nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
Two options:

Opaque integration akin to the current Caffe2’s ideep tensor. The tensor would support only a subset of operations that are explicitly implemented and fine-grained access of the tensor will not be efficient (e.g. operator[]). This is how e.g. sparse tensors are supported today. Note, that TensorImpl doesn’t need to be virtualized for it as top-level tensor operations (including resize_ and all math/nn ops) go through the dispatch mechanism (in TensorMethods.h and a few other places) and can be routed to another implementation.
Fine grained integration where PyTorch has visibility into what MKLDNN layout is. In this case majority of tensor ops would work and even many regular PT kernels would work against mkldnn tensors if they rely on TensorAccessor and friends. It’s a more powerful integration and provides a better UX but it’d require “opening the covers” for MKLDNN and also higher complexity for core PT code to recognize other layouts.

🚀 Feature
extend torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() to mimic python's tracemalloc.get_traced_memory(), where a user can reset the peak gauge at any point in their code. Probably a similar function with another name will be needed.
Example of how this works in tracemalloc:
import tracemalloc, numpy as np

def consume_cpu_ram(n): return np.ones((n, n))
def consume_cpu_ram_128mb(): return consume_cpu_ram(2**12)

# push the process' peak gauge high up and then release the memory
z = [consume_cpu_ram_128mb() for i in range(8)] # 1GB
del z

tracemalloc.start()

# expecting peak requirements of 256MB, and final 128MB
a1 = consume_cpu_ram_128mb()
a2 = consume_cpu_ram_128mb()
del a1

cpu_current, cpu_peak = list(map(lambda x: int(x/2**20), tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()))
tracemalloc.stop()

print(cpu_current, cpu_peak)

Output:
128 256

So now we can tell the profiled section of a code consumed 128MB, but it peaked at 256MB.
So pytorch could do exactly the same, here is some pseudo-code:
class max_memory_allocated_local():
    def start(self):
        self.begin = memory_allocated()
        max_memory_allocated_local_reset() # put the peak gauge to zero
    def stop(self):
        self.end  = memory_allocated()
        self.peak = max_memory_allocated_local()
    def get_traced_memory(self):    
        return self.end-self.begin, self.peak-self.begin

it introduces a local max_memory_allocated_local, which can be reset by the user, but otherwise working the same as max_memory_allocated().
Motivation
torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() is currently only useful for measuring the max memory ever allocated in a given process. If some memory is released it stops being useful for monitoring peak memory consumption in part of the code.
Pitch
Alternatives
Currently to accomplish this I have to start a thread that measures peak memory by samping used gpu ram every 0.001 sec, which is inefficient and imprecise.
Additional context
Initial discussion with more examples including my current workaround here:
https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/measuring-peak-memory-usage-tracemalloc-for-pytorch/34067/6

For large tensors (1e7 values in one dimension) torch.unique performs badly, if return_inverse=True is set.

    device = 'cuda:0' if use_cuda else 'cpu'
    for high in torch.logspace(1, 5, 5):
        high = int(high.item())
        print('Timing unique with high={} for {} values on {}'.format(
            high, N, device))
        x = torch.randint(low=0, high=high, size=(N,))
        if use_cuda:
            x = x.to(device)

        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        start = time.time()
        if use_dim:
            unique, inv = torch.unique(
                x, sorted=False, return_inverse=True, dim=0)
        else:
            unique, inv = torch.unique(x, sorted=False, return_inverse=True)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        print(time.time()-start)

nodes.bodyText: The contract for users using PyTorch JIT modules is that they can disable gradients by using the NoGradGuard in the thread that invokes torch::jit::Method(). This is a thread local variable and hence we need to be careful if our inference calls use multithreaded execution underneath since this contract might be violated if we don't propagate this thread local setting appropriately. We should ensure that this contract is respected when users use torch.jit.fork() and torch.jit.wait().

class GradCam:
def init(self, model, target_layer_names, use_cuda):
self.model = model
self.model.eval()
self.cuda = use_cuda
if self.cuda:
self.model = model.cuda()
	self.extractor = ModelOutputs(self.model, target_layer_names)

def forward(self, input):
	return self.model(input)

def __call__(self, input, index = None):
	if self.cuda:
		features, output = self.extractor(input.cuda())
	else:
		features, output = self.extractor(input)

	if index == None:
		index = np.argmax(output.cpu().data.numpy())

	one_hot = np.zeros((1, output.size()[-1]), dtype=np.float32)
	one_hot[0][index] = 1
	one_hot = Variable(torch.from_numpy(one_hot), requires_grad=True)
	if self.cuda:
		one_hot = torch.sum(one_hot.cuda() * output)
	else:
		one_hot = torch.sum(one_hot * output)

	nn.Sequential(*list(self.model.children())[0]).zero_grad()
	nn.Sequential(*list(self.model.children())[1]).zero_grad()
	one_hot.backward()

	grads_val = self.extractor.get_gradients()[-1].cpu().data.numpy()

	target = features[-1]
	target = target.cpu().data.numpy()[0, :]

	weights = np.mean(grads_val, axis = (2, 3))[0, :]
	cam = np.zeros(target.shape[1 : ], dtype = np.float32)

	for i, w in enumerate(weights):
		cam += w * target[i, :, :]

class GuidedBackpropReLU(Function):
def forward(self, input):
    positive_mask = (input > 0).type_as(input)
    output = torch.addcmul(torch.zeros(input.size()).type_as(input), input, positive_mask)
    self.save_for_backward(input, output)

def backward(self, grad_output):
    input, output = self.saved_tensors
    grad_input = None

    positive_mask_1 = (input > 0).type_as(grad_output)
    positive_mask_2 = (grad_output > 0).type_as(grad_output)
    grad_input = torch.addcmul(torch.zeros(input.size()).type_as(input), torch.addcmul(torch.zeros(input.size()).type_as(input), grad_output, positive_mask_1), positive_mask_2)

    return grad_input
